💡 Key Takeaways
  • Try not to get whole armies of Space Marines pasted against the surfaces of planets thanks to your shoddy tactics, please.
  • The stream showed off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss.
  • It has been revealed that each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Try not to get whole armies of Space Marines pasted against the surfaces of planets thanks to your shoddy tactics, please. So ask the bosses of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, who're keen not to have their training workloads doubled because you're a crap general and have gotten a tight-knit force of uber-tough grunts killed unnecessarily, hope as they watch you play. This and other things have been emphasised by a fresh stream showing off over an hour of campaigning in the strategy warhammerer.

The stream showed off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss. Described as a middle-of-the-road option in terms of system size, Praevoss is home to three conquerable planets and a couple of others that aren't suitable for stompy unit hijinks.

It has been revealed that each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over. "First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," the devs explained. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start [point], [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do." Creative assembly have also been able to play around a bit more with difficulty as a result of this setup.

Recent findings suggest that as the stream properly got going, the devs focused on chatting about unit specialisation, fleet movement, fleet actions, fleet transportation and Space Marine fleet buildings. Your fleet takes the form of big ships which can be parked above a continent on a planet and offer support via reinforcements and bombardment. As far as the Space Marines specifically go, they're designed to be a small force that's tough to kill, rather than a massive one that's able to recover more promptly and aims to overwhelm with sheer numbers as part of its gameplan.

According to recent reports, "Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the devs said, as if sensing some blunder I might make far in the future. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that." At least it looks like I'll not be losing any ships too, since their presence seems limited to providing support to the ground troops, rather than battling each other high above the planets.

As of right now, Total War: Warhammer 40,000 remains without a release date, but can be wishlisted on Steam if you fancy.

#154764. Wait, How Many People Left Can Actually Win Survivor 51?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1117 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cinemablend ↗ Open Full Page

Wait, How Many People Left Can Actually Win Survivor 51?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cinemablend

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’m not sure if you’ve noticed, but Survivor 51 is running out of main characters.
  • It has been revealed that jeff Probst has mentioned in the past that there’s no one size fits all winner’s edit on Survivor.
  • I’m not saying the person who wins every season is the person with the most confessionals or the person with the most sympathetic edit, but one recurring theme is that the winner is always a consistent and active part of the narrative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’m not sure if you’ve noticed, but Survivor 51 is running out of main characters. We’ve somehow lost four of the biggest, loudest and most vibrant personalities in consecutive weeks, and now, we’re suddenly left with a season that has a few main characters, a couple wacky side characters and a bunch of people who have been consistently deprioritized and underedited throughout the season. What is going on? How many of these castaways can actually even win?

It has been revealed that jeff Probst has mentioned in the past that there’s no one size fits all winner’s edit on Survivor. That’s both true and misleading. The longtime host and showrunner is correct in that the winner gets a different story based on their personality and what happened out there (the underdog, the challenge beast, the social threat, etc), but there is one very consistent pattern we do see: screentime.

I’m not saying the person who wins every season is the person with the most confessionals or the person with the most sympathetic edit, but one recurring theme is that the winner is always a consistent and active part of the narrative. The show goes out of their way to give us their perspective on what’s going on because the ultimate payoff needs to feel earned and it needs to make sense. That’s just storytelling 101. If we want to know, for example, why someone on the jury does or doesn’t vote for them at the end, it helps if we’re given context and confessionals about their relationship.

Unfortunately, with nine players left in Survivor 51, there are a ton of players who just aren’t present enough in the edit to seem like viable winners. Seriously, let’s run them down real quick. Cristian has been a little more prominent lately, but he had two confessionals during the first four episodes combined. Despite allegedly being so close to Sharonda that he told her about Carter’s idol, we haven’t seen that relationship developed in the slightest. This season would make no sense if he won.

It also wouldn’t make any sense if Thien An won. She’s in last place in total confessionals amongst the players left by an absolute mile. Why? I have no idea. She seems to have great social relationships and is an engaging and sometimes cutting confessionalist when she does get a chance to speak, but she’s the least present character in many episodes for unclear reasons. Why would they do that if she won?

According to recent reports, mike and Eric have been much more present parts of the edit, but their storylines have both been about how much everyone else is annoyed with them. Eric has been getting a wacky theater kid edit that has included multiple montages of him talking and everyone else being annoyed by it. There have maybe been ten shots of characters literally rolling their eyes after he talks. Mike is a different version of the same situation. He’s been the subject of numerous confessionals from other players about how he’s a “bottom feeder” and impossible to work with. I don’t see why Survivor would portray its winner that way.

Sources indicate that that’s four of the remaining nine players who have seemingly no chance, and I’m not sure Maggie is in a good spot either. She seems to be one of the most well-liked and dangerous players on the entire island. No one would vote for Mike during the Duos Challenge because he was paired with her, and Jelly has dropped confessionals about how she can win if she gets to the end. But the edit also gave her very little credit for Linnea, even though it was her proposal, and she has just over half as many confessionals as Jelly does (24 to 46).

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

That leaves literally four players: Jelly, Devin, Sharonda and Carter. I’d normally write Carter off because he has two episodes with zero confessionals and no player since Survivor 41 has won with even a single zero confessional episode, but as you can see, we’re a little short on viable winner possibilities. I’m out here trying to make excuses for people’s edits and see some silver lining showing why they could win. I think Carter can win. He’s at least been pretty present during the majority of the season. We’ve gotten his viewpoint consistently, and we’ve gotten confessionals from other people that speak of him very highly.

In a recent development, so, yeah, Carter is a maybe, but really, that leaves us with Jelly, Devin and Sharonda. The Helicopter Alliance has been the most consistent narrative throughline of the entire season, which is why it makes sense that these three are at the top of the list. Jelly and Devin have, without question, been the main characters of 52 (at least since Brady left), and they’re dominating in screentime and confessionals at 46 and 45 respectively. That’s twelve more than Eric, who is in third place of those remaining thanks to a bunch of vampire analogies and references to his fiance Gina.

Industry observers note that sharonda is quite a bit behind with 29 confessionals. Like Carter, there are some concerns with her edit, as there have been stretches where she hasn’t been super prominent, but her content has been so overwhelmingly positive that I’m willing to give her a pass. I still consider her a very viable winner at this point, as she should come into further prominence in the edit once the other players find out she’s been secretly working with Devin and Jelly the entire time.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t know who is going to win Survivor 52. There are three, maybe four viable candidates with Maggie and maybe Mike added in there as wild longshots. That’s a really small number of people in play for there being nine castaways left. In fact, it’s starting to feel a little like Survivor 49 where the entire fanbase was convinced one member of the Tres Leches alliance was going to win because they were the only people who seemed viable for like the entire second half of the game (apart from maybe Steven I guess).

Lack of winning edits aside and a few questionable twist-related decisions aside, Survivor 51 has been an absolute banger so far. Fingers crossed it’s able to stick the landing and fulfill its potential to be an all-time great season, whether one of these obvious contenders wins or not.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, by using auto drive in GTA 6 you get the opportunity to appreciate the level of detail your vehicle has, and how beautiful the world is around you, without the risk of slamming straight into the back of the next car as soon as you hit traffic. When you're not dealing with the controls yourself it can be quite relaxing to cruise around GTA 6, soaking up the sights and generally admiring everything Rockstar has created. To find out how it all works, here's how to enable auto drive in GTA 6.

Recent findings suggest that to use GTA 6 auto drive, you need to be in control of a vehicle and have a destination marker set on your map. From the vehicle, hold Down on the D-pad to access the camera options, then while still holding it press Options (PS5) or Menu (Xbox) to enter the CINEMATIC menu. You'll then see a prompt for ENABLE AUTO DRIVE in the bottom right corner, so hold the appropriate button to get it started.

According to recent reports, jason or Lucia will then begin driving on their own towards the destination, as the camera cycles through various cinematic views. You can use the right stick to move the camera around, and click R3/RS to switch to the next view. The triggers will also let you choose between three driving speeds, to determine how fast your driver will go, and you can change the destination marker on the map at any time to reroute.

We need to be clear that this is certainly not fast travel in GTA 6, as Jason or Lucia will obey all road rules and spend a lot of time sat in traffic, so it is instead intended as a way to soak up the atmosphere and get some great video footage or screenshots of your journey.

Also, be aware that auto drive in GTA 6 doesn't make everything perfect, and when I used it another driver hit my car then got out and started attacking it with a wrench! If something similar happens to you, then here's how to repair and fix your car in GTA 6.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You probably already know that your email isn't actually all that private, especially if you have a free account with a major service provider like Gmail (Google) or Outlook (Microsoft). But if you are sending sensitive information via email, you can minimize what can be snooped on and by whom using end-to-end encryption, which generally ensures that only the recipient can read your message. Here's what you need to know about email encryption and how to set up an extra layer of privacy.

According to recent reports, as this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Recent findings suggest that emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

According to recent reports, by contrast, with end-to-end encryption (E2EE), emails are readable only on the sender's and recipient's devices, and can be decrypted only with the recipient's private key. They're never translated into plaintext as they pass between and through servers to their destination, meaning that no one—including server providers, hackers, or law enforcement—can view the content. It's worth noting, though, that E2EE is not impenetrable nor a total guarantee of privacy. For example, metadata like subject lines and email addresses may remain in plaintext, and encrypted messages are still susceptible to phishing. Plus, forwarding an encrypted message breaks the encryption.

Recent findings suggest that still, end-to-end encryption is especially useful when sending sensitive information that may be valuable to bad actors, though if security and privacy are a high priority, you may want to consider it for all of your emails. How you deploy encryption depends on whether you are adding it to your current email or switching to a dedicated provider.

According to recent reports, if you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise people of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between people on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

The bottom line here is that email wasn't designed to be a highly secure form of communication. End-to-end encryption does add a layer of privacy and security if you jump through hoops to set it up, but it's still susceptible to human error and social engineering.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, rockstar has successfully shipped Grand Theft Auto 6, after years of work and more than a billion dollars spent.
  • According to recent reports, but that may not be enough to prevent layoffs at Rockstar, some people working within the studio fear.
  • "After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it's hard not to worry about what the future holds," Uriarte wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, rockstar has successfully shipped Grand Theft Auto 6, after years of work and more than a billion dollars spent. GTA 6 is already one of the highest-rated games ever - Eurogamer awarded it five stars in our GTA 6 review - and it's expected to be among the most successful, best-selling games ever.

According to recent reports, but that may not be enough to prevent layoffs at Rockstar, some people working within the studio fear. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer at Rockstar North, wrote about their concern for their job and those of their colleagues in an article on The Guardian.

"After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it's hard not to worry about what the future holds," Uriarte wrote. "It states a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.".

In a recent development, uriarte's piece comes as Rockstar staff's efforts to establish a union reach a critical point. A tribunal between the studio and fired IWBG union members just concluded, though the verdict may not arrive for many weeks or months.

According to recent reports, rockstar's UK studios are presently voting on recognising an official Rockstar workers union. Uriarte is in support of it and has urged colleagues to vote in favour of it. Results of that vote are expected today.

"Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that," Uriarte pointed out.

"As one of the biggest and most influential game studios in the world, what happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry - one in which workers' voices are taken into account more.".

Across its 12 offices around the world, Rockstar's headcount grew to 4,711 during GTA 6's development - double its size when it released Red Dead Redemption 2.

As popular and profitable as Rockstar's games are, the company has initiated layoffs in the past after shipping a major project. While there's no way of knowing whether the same is going to happen for GTA 6, the justifiable concerns - given the current state of the industry - are there. According to the ASGC Games Industry Layoffs Tracker, more than 12,000 developers have lost their jobs this year so far, up from more than 9,000 people last year.

#154759. They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2443 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2443 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display.
  • Sources indicate that likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap.
  • The point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've noted it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

Sources indicate that likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

The point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

We'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

That means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

The problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a big, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Sources indicate that chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

With that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

Sources indicate that while we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to revision the image. Like I said, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of crucial ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

The "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

Pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

Industry observers note that for what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

After a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

All of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

If that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a new player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

Recent findings suggest that so, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

According to recent reports, indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

Recent findings suggest that both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

Recent findings suggest that over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

It has been revealed that however, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot upcoming thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

Industry observers note that in both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the newly introduced PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

Early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

When it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint issue in bright ambient light.

Recent findings suggest that if you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

It has been revealed that not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the new RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

According to recent reports, just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

The long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint issue. But as I peck out these words on the fresh 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

Recent findings suggest that anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of issues like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

Industry observers note that really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The big brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, presently, be entirely sure about that.

Recent findings suggest that second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

I'd just stolen my very first airplane in GTA 6 and was happily cruising over the city when I looked out my window and saw an enormous purple building. I banked, slowed down, and flew a bit closer to read the huge sign on the roof.

It has been revealed that oh, hell yes. I was so excited to throw my carefully accumulated three hundred dollars away on poker and slots that I immediately attempted my very first landing. After the explosion and my miraculous resurrection, I rushed back to the casino and crashed again, this time with my body into the locked front doors.

According to recent reports, the casino in GTA 6 is closed. Trust me, I tried every door, and the only one that opened was a utility closet.

I was early into my playthrough, still in Chapter 1 of the GTA 6 story missions, so I thought maybe there'll be some mission that unlocks the casino so I can play some poker, try my luck at the slots, and maybe bet on the also-closed dog track—I assume it's a dog track because I've seen dogs in GTA 6, but no horses—that's right next door to the casino.

Sources indicate that nope! I'm now 100% done with the main story and that casino is still closed. And that's not the only business in GTA 6 that isn't open for business. Not even a half-mile away from the casino there's a go-cart track called Hot Skidz sporting a huge "Coming Soon" sign. I saw that early in my game as well, and checked back later. Still closed. I also found a second, smaller casino. Also closed.

Sources indicate that what a letdown. I managed to get my motorcycle onto the go-cart track, and as I drove glumly around it, alone, having no fun, I perked up a bit. Maybe this just gives me something to look forward to. A hint of more singleplayer content that'll be coming to GTA 6 next year. Hopefully next year.

There's already a lot of seemingly unfinished stuff in GTA 6, partial systems that could be added to and completed, like:.

I felt better after that, but as I went back to stare at that huge, closed casino—which is all lit up at night like it's actually open, even though it is not open, and I know this because I rechecked all the doors—I remembered how the casino in GTA 5 worked. It came to the game post launch, but only as part of GTA Online. It never opened in singleplayer.

In a recent development, but surely, why include the building at all in GTA 6 singleplayer if it wasn't also going to be in singleplayer? They wouldn't do that to us, would they? They wouldn't open it in GTA 6 Online and not open it in GTA 6 singleplayer.

According to recent reports, that would be like putting dozens of dogs in a game and not letting us have our own dog. Madness.

#154757. Here Are Some Super Useful Control Shortcuts GTA 6 Doesn’t Tell You About

Here Are Some Super Useful Control Shortcuts GTA 6 Doesn’t Tell You About

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Kotaku

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve played over 150 hours of Grand Theft Auto 6.
  • According to recent reports, first off, let’s start with the whole reason I wanted to write this blog.
  • It has been revealed that I had no idea you could do this until I saw people sharing it on Reddit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6GTA 6Rockstar Games.

I’ve played over 150 hours of Grand Theft Auto 6. You might think I’ve seen it all, and that I know everything there is to know about the game. Nope! I’m still discovering new mechanics, features, and open-world moments after all this time. This includes some very handy control shortcuts I recently learned about that will make your life in Vice City a little easier.

According to recent reports, first off, let’s start with the whole reason I wanted to write this blog. Did you know that you can promptly toggle your car radio on and off without having to enter a submenu? All you have to do is double-tap left on the D-pad, and Jason or Lucia will turn the radio on or off.

It has been revealed that I had no idea you could do this until I saw people sharing it on Reddit. The game doesn’t explain this shortcut, as far as I can tell. I couldn’t even find it mentioned in the in-game help menu, which does include lots of other nifty tips and tricks.

Here’s another trick I just learned about: You can double-tap the circle/B button while in a car to cycle the headlights between off, high beams, and low beams.

Industry observers note that I thought you had to hold left on the D-pad to open up the vehicle submenu to turn off the headlights, but nope! And again, this isn’t mentioned in the help menu and if a prompt appeared during the normal course of the game to explain this, I and many others must have missed it.

Here’s another useful thing you can do inside cars: If you double-tap the triangle/Y button while driving, you’ll exit the vehicle without turning off the engine or radio.

GTA 6‘s help menu does call this out and mentions you can do this at speed to have your car drive into something while you roll out the side to safely. But again, I can’t remember a single time when the game forced me to do this or taught me that it was possible. I learned from a random post online. I guess I should have dug through the help menu more, but come on, who is doing that in Grand Theft Auto?

Another feature mentioned in the help menu that I just learned about is the ability to click the right stick in and yell at nearby drivers. Rockstar refers to this as the road rage button, and it’s a good thing to have in a game where NPC drivers, inspired by real Floridian drivers, suck shit and drive like maniacs.

One more useful control trick: You can double-tap the triangle/Y button while driving a boat to get up and walk around the deck while the boat keeps on cruising.

Sources indicate that the next time I boot up GTA 6, I’m going to start double-tapping random buttons during different parts of the game to see what other hidden shortcuts and control options Rockstar has buried in this massive game. The search for secrets in World of Warcraft: Forever continues ever onwards, with a latest breakthrough coming to light in recent days. The latest discovery? An elusive new cat that can be tamed by hunters in one of the game's new zones.

The cat's name is Ta'Shkal, and they can be found on Mount Hyjal. An endgame levelling zone, players will have to reach at least level 57 in order to safely make their way up there and recruit this upcoming pet.

Sources indicate that the way you do so is relatively simple. You need to find a small corrupted cat figuring within the Felblood Scar region of Mount Hyjal. Once you've found that, you then need to travel up to a hidden lantern south of the Mourning's Rest area. With the figurine in your bags, you'll be able to interact with the lantern, spawning the cat for you to tame (granted you're playing a hunter).

So what's the big deal about this cat? Well, aside from the fact it's got a strange colour scheme of green fur with orange stripes, the cat also has a base attack speed of 1.0. This means it'll attack once every second, which is pretty fast and allows for greater damage output from your pet. This inherently makes the pet valuable for endgame hunter players, who are looking to improve their performance in PvE and PvP.

This is not the only secret discovered by World of Warcraft: Forever sleuths. Last week, they pieced together a hidden quest chain that leads to two special swords. As of writing, only one has been found, though progress continues in pursuit of the second.

It has been revealed that the game has been out for just over two weeks now, and continues to prove popular among newly introduced and returning players. It's the biggest launch in the series' history, and has gone down well with people so far. Even if it has recently suffered its first controversy with a now-fixed gold exploit.

#154755. Breaking: Remembering the back alley brawls of The Warriors, a Rockstar city game that isn't an open world

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (944 w)

Breaking: Remembering the back alley brawls of The Warriors, a Rockstar city game that isn't an open world

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives.
  • According to recent reports, probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria.
  • There's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives. I've already gushed about the Starlight Zone in Sonic the Hedgehog – the mild dissociation incubated by the soft, ceaseless glare of the construction yard, the eyeless brick at the level's nadir, the sleepless glitter of the skyline. Now, let me wind the clock forward, and backward, to Rockstar Toronto's The Warriors. One long night from the late '70s, sweaty and electric and menacing, fed through dank and sullen polygons from 2005.

According to recent reports, probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria. Both the game and the movie open with a view of Coney Island's Wonder Wheel, its neon lamps forming a floating tracery of Morse code, cabins swinging almost imperceptibly against solid darkness. This is a kind of night in which light is more emblem than illumination, refusing to travel far, clinging to its source like a frightened ghost.

There's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6. I'd love a proper PC port of The Warriors, first, and not just because I like coming up with fancy ways to talk about Ferris wheels. A PC port would be a timely reminder that Rockstar used to make city games that aren't open worlds, city games made of levels, and were pretty good at it. The classic thrill of GTA is to jump into a car and circle the metropolis, radio on and arm dangling, snatches of pedestrian dialogue bursting in your wake as you zip through downtown, the skyscrapers streaming by and evaporating, the world your oyster. In The Warriors, the city is No Man's Land and the night is a tightly compartmentalised maze. Your goal is to reach the other side of it on your own two feet, before a thousand rival miscreants kick your head in.

Recent findings suggest that you lead a group of angry young guys of different ethnicities, wearing tribal colours and following a martial code - spiritual descendants of the stranded Greek soldiers of Xenephon's Anabais. Women barely feature in this relentlessly macho fable, and are mostly depicted as victims or seducers. Other genders are totally absent, while gay characters were considered for the film, but eventually cut. The game expands the storyline, filling in events before the titular Coney Island tearaways find themselves framed for a murder during an attempted city-wide gang uprising. But it otherwise adheres religiously to the movie's dingy and hyperbolic direction, hugging the visual language in ways that are slightly odd to return to, now that Rockstar have arguably outgrown their nerdy inferiority complex before the giants of cinema.

Recent findings suggest that the game's Fresh York is mysterious and sparsely populated: the only people abroad are other gangs and cops. The playable areas eschew affluent districts and pleasure zones; instead, you hop over a million chainlink fences in subway terminals and trashy alleyways. Most of the buildings are sealed and silent. The sky is a painted forest of chimneys, silos and stripped low cloud. You keep waiting for Batman to descend from the girders of a flyover; some of the enemy gangs certainly wouldn't look out of place in Rocksteady's Arkham. The murk isn't quite as pungent as you'd find in a PS1 flâneur like Urban Chaos, but it's respectably enveloping. I'd linger here, a plummy-accented tourist with a headful of references, cooing decorously over the stained and withdrawn shopfronts, were it not for the constant risk of getting stomped.

It has been revealed that back in the day, a few reviewers described The Warriors as having "deep" combat, offering a selection of directional jabs and kicks, grappling moves, terrain finishers and squad commands. I can't really see it. Certainly, The Warriors is no Sleeping Dogs. What the Warriors is is a believably chaotic brawler, with an enjoyable taste for friendly fire.

It has been revealed that you spot a couple other Warriors surrounded by face-painted Baseball Furies, and launch into a crossbody tackle that bowls the whole group over. You straddle one of the clowns and are about to punch his teeth out when a friend lobs a trash can at the both of you. Now black-eyed and bleeding, you seize a dropped bat and swing randomly into the mob of warring outfits. Insults, taunts, chair legs and beer bottles fly back and forth. It feels like a fight. The riot spills out over each map, onto rooftops and into any businesses that have unwisely decided to stay open late. Looking back, I can see the first inklings of those spectacular drunken bar scuffles in Red Dead Redemption 2, though nobody's packing heat. The almost total absence of guns is, of course, the other thing that makes The Warriors novel, if you come to it from GTA.

I've yet to play Rockstar's latest GTA, which is now available on console worldwide. I've yet to decide how it fits into my evolving half-arsed anthropology of videogame nightlife. Still, I've spent a fair amount of time looking at screenshots and videos, and I'm finding the nights too bright. Too bright! All those shades seeping everywhere, all those rays being traced, all the spotlights and sequins, the way everything glimmers or glistens – it's too heady for me. Send me back to 2005's Fresh York, where the darkness feels like it's part of the very mortar, and there's always a friend willing to "accidentally" hurl a bin at my head.

Industry News: 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that apple has a pretty good track record on privacy.
  • It has been revealed that enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device.
  • Sources indicate that another hack for maintaining privacy on public networks is to enable rotating MAC addresses, which randomizes the identifier your device broadcasts when scanning for and connecting to wifi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that apple has a pretty good track record on privacy. The company bakes a number of protections into its OSes to keep your data from being shared or stolen. That noted, you can make your Apple devices even more secure. There are plenty of opt-in settings that make it even harder for anyone to snoop on your device and activity. These are the best privacy hacks for your Mac.

It has been revealed that enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Sources indicate that another hack for maintaining privacy on public networks is to enable rotating MAC addresses, which randomizes the identifier your device broadcasts when scanning for and connecting to wifi. If you use either your real MAC address or a fixed one (random but unchanging), it's easier to track your activity on that network, including when you arrive, how long you stay, and when you leave. Rotating addresses are best for public, shared networks you temporarily connect to, and don't require a login via a captive portal (like hotel wifi). You can turn this on for specific networks via Settings > Wi-Fi > [Network Name] > Details and change Private Wi-Fi address to Rotating.

It has been revealed that images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for promptly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.).

Recent findings suggest that apple collects information about your device for diagnostic purposes or to improve apps and services, some of which is shared with third-party app developers. This may include crash and usage data as well as recordings and transcripts of Siri interactions and iCloud analytics. You can disable sharing for some or all of these categories under Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements.

It has been revealed that you may be surprised by the number of apps and system services that use your device's location in the background. You should definitely disable location services for third-party apps that don't require location to function. You can find these toggles under Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services. You can also turn off location permissions for some Apple apps and services if you're not using them on your device, like Weather and Maps. Finally, tap System Services and disable location for any non-essential features—at the very least, disable "Mac Analytics" and "Significant Locations & routes" (which lets your Mac and other iCloud devices learn locations and routes you use often).

Sources indicate that third-party apps on your Mac that need access to your device's camera and microphone have to request permission, and it's easy to grant this in the moment and then forget that you've allowed it. You should regularly audit which apps have these permissions and revoke access from those that don't need them on a day-to-day basis. Disabling them forces the app to ask again. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone or Camera to see the allowed apps and flip the toggle to disable permissions.

Another permission type you may have granted without much thought is local network access. This allows third-party apps to discover and communicate with other devices—printers, smart speakers, and IoT devices—on your home wifi. While this may be useful for services like Spotify that cast to connected hardware, other utilities, media apps, and games probably don't need to be mapping your network in the background. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network to audit permissions and disable those that aren't needed.

Industry observers note that another vital permission to check concerns third-party apps that have access to your Mac's full disk, which includes data from Mail, Messages, Safari, Home, Time Machine, and admin settings. If an app only works with files you explicitly open and save, it doesn't need full disk access. Legitimate use cases may include antivirus and malware scanners, productivity tools, or backup utilities that you trust. You can also audit which apps have access to specific files and folders. This is under Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access or Files & Folders.

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

The Body is available to stream right now with a Netflix subscription, and when I learned it was about controversy surrounding a Catholic school, I had to check it out. As someone who attended a Catholic grade school and high school, I was eager to see how it was portrayed, and while things were a bit wilder than I remember, the show really nailed two parts.

In a recent development, for those curious but still want to watch for themselves, I'll keep this spoiler-free. All readers really need to know going in is that this series surrounds a Catholic school dance team, and what happens when an initiation prank goes too far and a student's life is in danger.

According to recent reports, project Hail Mary was called "blatant Catholic propaganda," as described by someone who never watched, and similarly, The Body is being vilified by groups of concerned Catholics who have not and likely will not watch it. As someone who did, I'll admit no one should go into this assuming it'll be a family-friendly adventure, but the parts that handle religion are done with lots of care.

Recent findings suggest that I say this, especially, as a person who went through their teenage years in Catholic school. For many, your teens are going to be one of the most rebellious and potentially dangerous times of your lives. Imagine some of the wildest things you did in high school, and now imagine the feeling that you'll be eternally damned for it days afterward.

It has been revealed that "Catholic Guilt," they call it, is shown in full effect in The Body. Obviously, there are people in this who deserve to feel guilty, but there are also cases in which we see characters feel immense guilt or shame for things that would otherwise be quite normal today.

According to recent reports, some of this is due to The Body being set in 2004, when things like LGBTQ+ relationships weren't as prevalent in pop culture and were largely frowned upon in Catholic schools. Pregnant teens at my high school weren't allowed to walk to get their diploma at graduation, and I couldn't imagine what would happen if someone were openly gay back then.

According to recent reports, and yet these things happened, and these people existed. It's one of the things I love about The Body, and the way it navigates what would undoubtedly be a scary time for those individuals. Again, it was more extreme than anything I dealt with, but I know that feeling of guilt quite well.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

It has been revealed that I also think The Body does a great job of handling what goes down when something controversial does happen at a Catholic school. I can't get into specifics, but there was a controversy at my school so big that it received national attention, and the fact that it was a Catholic school only amplified the interest and headlines.

Sources indicate that the Internet Can’t Stop Talking About People’s Mouths In Netflix’s The Christmas Switch. I Can’t Unsee It.

Like the kids in The Body, a number of kids attending were from families of some renown. Families were willing to keep quiet about events occurring to protect their children, and the school was eager to let any controversy fade as swiftly as possible.

Recent findings suggest that there's certainly something to the added pressure of a Catholic school striving to be perfect. As The Body points out, any controversy draws the same critics who will immediately point to past incidents highlighted by the movie Spotlight. No one wants to be the person to bring added negative attention to the religion, but at the end of the day it's a high school full of rowdy teens just like any other.

In a recent development, I'm admittedly a lapsed Catholic, but I would say The Body was the best representation in media for the faith since Wake Up, Dead Man. In that, both deal with Catholicism, but not so much that they're openly mocking or blaspheming it. They're stories about the people who practice it, who are imperfect and flawed. I don't think teachers should show it in class, but it is worth a watch for those who are curious.

Check out The Body and other upcoming Netflix indicates as 2026 winds down. With the holidays right around the corner, there's nothing like watching something controversial to spark some conversation at the family dinner table!

In a recent development, epic Games are, as you're probably aware, going major on genAI at the moment. To the extent that, last month, the Tim Sweeney-helmed company declared the Epic AI MegaJam. Build a playable game in Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite with help from as many AI agents or tools as you like was the pitch.

So, naturally, sorting the submissions by 'Popular' turns up a game about a fish with a sniper rifle whose creator says they deliberately made it without using any generative AI.

Industry observers note that the game's called LSD:FIH and sees a cigarette-smoking bit of shoe-wearing marine life go full MLG and start pulling off trickshots on blobs. If you struggled to parse that, you'll probably struggle even more with developer PolyCube's description of it as being a "computer game about a fih aura-farming". "No AI was used to make this game," is the other line in their description, which is far easier to parse.

In a recent development, "I made a game for the Epic's 'vibe-coding gamejam' megajam without using any AI in four days," they expanded on not Bluesky. "Sorta ran out of time so gameplay didn't turn out how I wanted, but hey it's still pretty aura.".

According to recent reports, other submissions the megajam included a game called THIS GAME IS AI SLOP and one dubbed Goon Patrol - Director's Cut. If you're wondering how a game without genAI use could be allowed to stand among the slop masterpieces, it's because Epic ended up having to make clearer not long after the jam was declared that submissions didn't have to make use of genAI as a hard rule, leaving it up to the developer how much or little was worked in.

Still, I imagine noted genAI advocate Tim Sweeney's not best pleased that a game deliberately swimming against the slop tide shows up at the top if you hit up the Popular filter. The choice to sell pure or cut coke in GTA 6 comes around early in Chapter 3 as part of the "Dealer's Choice" mission, in which Boobie asks Jason to go get drugs from Tyrone and sell them on. Boobie seems happy for Jason to sell a less-than perfect product if it means higher profitability, but Dre'Quan has been warning you about overstepping constantly, suggesting that this might be less than wise. Below I'll explain all the outcomes of choosing the cut drugs or the pure stuff in Grand Theft Auto 6, as well as what the best choice actually is.

What appears to be a double choice in GTA 6 to sell the pure or cut drugs can actually split three ways, as selling the cut drugs leads to a second choice: when you get found out, are you still going to demand the same price for worse coke?

Here's all three outcomes in GTA 6, though keep in mind that any financial gain is earned later after the mission when Boobie sends your cut of the money to you.

Sources indicate that we've yet to play out all the outcomes, but it seems as though the highest payment comes from selling the pure stuff, which is $1,500 - not a lot anyway. Nonetheless, we'll update this guide if we find out more.

In a recent development, the reality is that this is not a hugely significant choice beyond the possibility of a shootout. The money that Boobie sends you later doesn't seem to be significantly impacted and there's no long-term story impacts, though you can marginally increase your profits by looting any enemies you encounter on the third option.

Recent findings suggest that still, I would choose the first option and sell pure for the best outcome, as it's the cleanest. That being remarked, the differences in reward are so minor that if you're out to make money fast in GTA 6, this quest doesn't make a huge difference either way.

Grand Theft Auto 6 has been out in the hands of console players for a few days now, and a few of us at PC Gamer have been dusting off our PlayStations and Xboxes to dive into Leonida as we eagerly anticipate its eventual (but yet unannounced) PC release next year potentially.

I've been gaming it up myself and, as is always the case with GTA, I am absolutely loving driving around. Flying down the highway, exploring all the alleyways and retail areas, and taking out to the waters on a boat or jetski. All of it, of course, to the soundtrack of GTA 6's various radio stations.

It has been revealed that there are a huge number of stations in this game—19 of them, to be exact—with a ton of excellently-curated songs lingering within and famous cameo hosts. Usually I find myself just picking one station and sticking to it, but with GTA 6? I've been cycling between quite a few, each one offering something a little bit different.

In a recent development, four stations have been grabbing most of my attention though. Pop station Flash FM has easily gained the most airtime in my playthrough so far. Am I listening to Ariana Grande in my everyday life? No. But am I bombing it down the highway while singing Break Free to myself every time it comes on? I absolutely am.

Industry observers note that but I've also been peppering in a ton of 80s station Vice City FM. I mean, c'mon, you've got Weird Al Yankovic as a co-host, first of all. But you've also got straight up bangers like Lionel Richie's All Night Long, Simply Red's Money's Too Tight (To Mention), and Billy Ocean's Loverboy.

There's also Emotion 98.3, the radio station dedicated to songs about love (both being in love and being heartbroken, of course) and yes, I have stayed in the car waiting to hear Phil Collins' excellent drumming in In The Air Tonight. And finally, because I am a raging emo at heart, I've obviously had to whack on a bunch of The Chamber 106.6. Tool, System of a Down, and Metallica? Count me in.

It has been revealed that but what about you? If any of you PC gamers are partaking on console, is only one radio station catching your attention, or have you found yourself channel hopping just like me? Or is there somehow not a single station that's caught your fancy, instead finding the podcasts a more entertaining use of your listening time? Be sure to drop a comment and let me know.

Breaking: GameStop CEO slams 'code-in-a-box' games in the wake of GTA 6's discless release

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ryan Cohen, CEO of GameStop - the self-proclaimed "world's largest retail gaming and trade-in destination" - is not happy with the emerging trend of games releasing without discs.
  • In an interview with Bloomberg, Cohen explained: "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend.
  • Recent findings suggest that these comments come in the wake of GTA 6's launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ryan Cohen, CEO of GameStop - the self-proclaimed "world's largest retail gaming and trade-in destination" - is not happy with the emerging trend of games releasing without discs. Per the CEO, the industry's move away from physical games and towards a digital-only future is harmful to both consumers and businesses.

In an interview with Bloomberg, Cohen explained: "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend. Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it’s also hurt GameStop.".

Recent findings suggest that these comments come in the wake of GTA 6's launch. The game, expected to be the biggest video game launch of all time, is not shipping on discs at all. Even if you purchase a physical copy of the game, what you will actually take home is a 'code in a box' - giving you a code you can redeem on your console of choice that entitles you to a digital version of the game. GTA 6 is not the first game to do this, but it is the most high-profile. Similarly to discs, codes are also region-locked (at least on the PS5), meaning that the proliferation of codes as a format isn't even helping make games more readily available in certain markets.

Cohen notes he's been in conversation with "the obvious [publishers]" but that he's had little sway on their plans. "Of course they don’t like [trade-ins] because removing a used copy eliminates an alternative to buying latest," he told Bloomberg. "They're taking away competition.".

Though Cohen doesn't name GTA 6 specifically in the Bloomberg interview, it's clear that he's talking about Rockstar's megaton launch (he explicitly tweeted "GTA. On a disc. In a case. On your shelf. Like if you still want a physical copy" two days ago). The lack of trade-in potential is clearly harming his business; the Bloomberg article reveals pre-owned and refurbished products make up 22% of the GameStop's sales, down 32 percent from the same time a year ago.

Of course, the proliferation of game-in-a-box products doesn't end with GTA 6. Sony aims to stop producing physical discs for new PlayStation games starting in January 2028, moving to a digital-only model despite pushback from consumers and certain developers and publishers. The outcry is doing little to influence Sony's decision, however.

Disc or no disc, GTA 6 is expected to cross $2bn in its opening weekend, and at the moment that is looking like a conservative figure, too. It's estimated the game has sold well over 19.05m units at the time of writing. Despite the astronomical sales, though, employees at Rockstar are still worried about layoffs. Additionally, a tribunal between the studio and fired IWBG union members (who were fired for apparent breaches of their NDAs) just concluded, though the verdict may not arrive for many weeks or months.

If you need a hand with any of the myriad things GTA 6 asks you to do, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, panache Digital Games will release the first major content enhancement for the Early Access version of dark third-person narrative action adventure game 1666: Amsterdam in December, the developer confirmed. It will expand the game’s world, story, and supernatural abilities.

The December revision marks the first major expansion of the Early Access experience, bringing newly introduced areas to explore, new supernatural abilities, and another Original for players to confront.

A Newly introduced Region, a New Original, and More Witchcraft.

Arriving during the final moon of the year, the first major patch marks the beginning of a series of planned expansions for 1666: Amsterdam.

Players will be able to explore Ouderkerk, a newly introduced region slightly larger than the game’s at the moment available area, effectively doubling the world players can explore. Alongside this new location comes another Esbat and a new Original, bringing the next chapter of Noa’s journey to Early Access.

The upgrade will also introduce additional Lux and Nux spells and combos, along with upcoming jewels and potions, giving players more ways to develop their abilities and approach encounters.

Panache Digital Games will share more details about these additions in the weeks leading up to the December release.

■ Early Access Price Remains Unchanged.

Panache Digital Games has also confirmed that 1666: Amsterdam will remain at its current Early Access price when the December enhancement launches, with no price increase for the new content.

This first major revision is part of the team’s ongoing Early Access roadmap, with further expansions planned as development continues.

1666: Amsterdam is available now in Early Access for PC via Steam and Epic Games Store.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ubisoft have laid off 166 developers, with this latest round of cuts at the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry publishers taking place at two of their studios in Eastern Canada.
  • Both IGN and GamesIndustry.biz report that the cuts, which amount to just under 4% studios' total combined headcount, affected staff working on recently cancelled or significantly changed projects.
  • "Ubisoft is reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations," Ubisoft noted in a statement handed to both sites.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ubisoft have laid off 166 developers, with this latest round of cuts at the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry publishers taking place at two of their studios in Eastern Canada. Both studios affected, Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Quebec, had a hand in last year's Assassin's Creed Shadows, with Montreal especially being a major and long-tenured development hub for the firm.

Both IGN and GamesIndustry.biz report that the cuts, which amount to just under 4% studios' total combined headcount, affected staff working on recently cancelled or significantly changed projects.

"Ubisoft is reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations," Ubisoft noted in a statement handed to both sites. "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

It has been revealed that "We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues. We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources.".

Sources indicate that ubisoft Montreal are at the moment working on Assassin’s Creed Hexe, reportedly a witchy tale set during the time of the Holy Roman Empire, which switched creative directors earlier this ear and is one of the games Ubi are keen to get out of the door. What Quebec have been up to since Shadows shipped is less clear. They're a much smaller than Montreal and were founded in 2005.

In a recent development, ubisoft have been carrying out mass cuts across their studios worldwide all the way through this year. Ubisoft Singapore and Trials developers Redlynx. Ubisoft Winnipeg, Belgrade, and Barcelona. Long-time Tom Clancy studio Red Storm. Ubisoft's Paris HQ. Three German studios including Anno devs Ubisoft Mainz. All have been subjected to some form of cuts or closure.

Meanwhile. changes to remote working policies have also contributed to strikes at Ubisoft studios in France and Italy.

Solidarity to all of the Ubisoft workers who've been affected by these layoffs in Montreal and Quebec.

Industry observers note that is there something going on today? A lot of talk about committing crimes and the like, I just can't quite put my finger on why… Ah well, couldn't be important or interesting. What is interesting, however, is Keepsake County, a "midwestern stealth game" that has rolled out on this inauspicious day about stealing stuff from "hideous farmhouses in the middle of nowhere.".

Sources indicate that with the sarcastic intro out the way, I will address the elephant in the room: Vovly's Adventure: Reslimed is out today too. Fine, fine, yes I know GTA 6 is the game everyone's talking about, but Forward Instinct, the devs behind Keepsake County, seem well aware of that in their launch day post for the game: "Folks, thanks for your incredible patience. Keepsake County is finally OUT! And yes, it is deeply ironic that it wound up being today, of all days, that we got the green light to finally release, but here we are.".

In a recent development, keepsake Country was supposed to release earlier this month, but seemingly got caught up in the backlog Valve are faced with that's undoubtedly been caused by genAI games. In any case, the burgle-em-up does look quite delightful. I'm not sure if I can quite put my finger on exactly why I get this feeling, but it calls to mind a more complex version of the kind of game you'd find on Cartoon Network's website back in the day (which is a high point of praise, I'd like to be clear).

Sources indicate that each house in Keepsake Country is procedurally generated, meaning you never quite know what to expect when you enter. There's lockpicking, resident tie upping, and of course stealing to be done, but it doesn't just stop at the house. Parking your car, for instance, is an important thing to consider; do you want it hidden so you're less likely to be discovered, or right at the front door so you can make a speedy escape? Not to mention you have to deal with the fuzz showing up at some point if you aren't quick enough!

Sources indicate that gear and the like can be improved between runs, meaning you can lockpick faster or delay the cops, it all seems quite systemically thoughtful. Very much some immersive sim vibes from this one, just on a much smaller scale. And most certainly worth considering picking up on a release day like today! If you're interested in doing so, you can pick it up on Steam right here.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The internet of today is a far cry from the days when Grand Theft Auto 5 was released, which is partly why Rockstar didn't bring back its own satirical version of the web in GTA 6.
  • It has been revealed that the web pages of Lifeinvadder, Bleeter, and Eyefind have instead given way to BuckMe, Scooter Bros, and WhatUp apps.
